title: Magnon damping as a probe of Kondo coupling in magnetically ordered systems

paper_content.abstract: In d-electron systems, there can also be intricate interplay between Kondo coupling and magnetic interactions as that in f-electron systems, but the underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, using inelastic neutron scattering, we investigate the temperature evolution of the low-energy spin waves (magnons) in a metallic van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3−xGeTe2, and observe that the magnon damping diverges at both low and high temperatures and exhibits a minimum at an intermediate temperature. These behaviours are described by a formula that combines logarithmic and power-law terms, representing the dominant contributions from Kondo coupling and thermal fluctuations, respectively. These findings can be explained by considering electron-magnon scattering of spin-flip type within the ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg lattice model, distinct from the original Kondo effect which only considers the coupling between itinerant electrons and isolated impurity spins. These results unveil the intriguing interplay between itinerant electrons and spin waves in metallic 3d-electron systems with magnetic order, and provide magnon damping as a new effective probe of Kondo coupling in metallic quantum magnets, thereby opening new avenues for exploring Kondo physics from the magnon perspective.
paper_content.introduction:
The original Kondo effect in dilute magnetic alloys, which takes the resistivity minimum as one of the characteristics, describes the scattering of conduction electrons by magnetic impurities in such systems [1, 2]. This effect is classified as the single-impurity Kondo problem and is now well understood based on the spin-flip scatterings of conduction electrons off the single-impurity spins (Fig. 1a) [1, 2]. The concept of Kondo physics has been extended to include the correlated electron systems, specifically those consisting of a dense periodic array of local moments interacting with the conduction electron sea through an antiferromagnetic Kondo interaction, referred to as a Kondo lattice (Fig. 1b-d) [2–5]. The Kondo-lattice model was initially proposed to describe the heavy-fermion state in f-electron systems, particularly in intermetallics containing Ce, Yb, or U elements [2–7]. The competition between the Kondo effect and couplings of localized spins underlies various intriguing phenomena in these heavy-fermion compounds (Fig. 1e), including quantum criticality [8–11], strange-metal behaviour [11, 12], magnetism [13–16] and superconductivity[17, 18], which can be tuned by chemical doping, magnetic field or pressure [8–12]. In the strong Kondo coupling regime, the hybridization between localized f electrons and conduction electrons leads to the quenching of local moments and the expansion of the Fermi surface, resulting in the formation of a heavy Fermi-liquid state (Fig. 1c,d) [2–7, 19, 20]. Magnetic order can arise when the strength of the effective magnetic interaction between localized spins exceeds the Kondo coupling. Moreover, the coexistence of magnetic order with Kondo effect [13–16] or superconductivity [17, 18] can be observed, particularly in systems where the duality of f electrons emerges due to the mixed-valence situation and the multiorbital nature [13–18].

More recently, the unexpected heavy-fermion state has also been observed in certain d-electron transition metals, which reside in the intermediate regime between itineracy and localization of d electrons [21–31]. Understanding magnetism within the framework of this duality and the applicability of the Kondo-lattice model to such systems are currently active topics of research [21, 23, 25–31]. The van der Waals (vdW) metallic ferromagnet Fe3−xGeTe2 is one such example material [29–35]. Due to the coexistence of localized and itinerant 3d electrons, there are conflicting reports regarding the microscopic origin of the magnetism in Fe3−xGeTe2 [29–32, 36–39]. In our earlier work, we have reconciled the debate by showing that the ferromagnetism has a dual origin, with local moments and itinerant electrons contributing to the low-energy spin waves and columnlike continua, respectively [31]. Moreover, there is accumulating evidence for the Kondo coupling between these two components, such as the Fano resonance feature [29, 30], large effective electron mass [29, 34, 37], and the incoherent-coherent crossover in transport and magnetic measurements [29]. In particular, the resistivity curve of Fe3−xGeTe2 reveals a slope change at a characteristic temperature of approximately 90 K, as depicted in Fig. 1d. Below this temperature, the Kondo-lattice behaviour emerges in the magnetic ordering phase, accompanied by the enhancement of Fermi surface volume and effective electron mass [29]. Notably, this resistivity behaviour aligns with observations in other d-electron systems exhibiting a heavy-fermion state [22, 24, 25], but is distinct from either the Kondo-impurity model or the Kondo lattice in f-electron systems (Fig. 1d). Since our earlier work has indicated that Kondo screening significantly enhances spin-wave damping at 4 K compared to 100 K [31], a question naturally arises: will the damping follow certain scaling behaviour due to the Kondo coupling effect?

Here we report inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements on the temperature evolution of low-energy spin waves in Fe-deficient Fe3−xGeTe2 single crystals with Curie temperature TC ∼ 160 K. Upon cooling from TC, we observe that the magnon damping rate initially decreases, reaching a minimum around T∗d ∼ 90 K, before rapidly increasing again. This behaviour follows a scaling relation combining both logarithmic and power-law terms. Additionally, we find that the in-plane Kondo coupling is stronger than the out-of-plane coupling, resulting in a softening of in-plane magnons at low temperatures. Using the state-of-the-art tensor-network algorithm [40–45], we reproduce the observed magnon damping minimum and logarithmic scaling within a ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg (FMKH) model. Although the form is analogous to the original Kondo effect describing the coupling between itinerant electrons and impurity spins [1, 2], the underlying mechanism is essentially different — here, itinerant d electrons scatter the collective excitations of local moments via a spin-flip process induced by Kondo coupling. Our results provide compelling evidence for the existence of Kondo effect in the metallic ferromagnet Fe3−xGeTe2, and demonstrate magnon damping as an effective probe for the Kondo coupling in systems where magnetic order and Kondo effect coexist.
paper_content.results:
Damping rate minimum and logarithmic scaling

Figure 2a,b shows the energy scans at various temperatures for the off-centered in-plane and out-of-plane positions, respectively. As no sizable spin gap was observed at the zone center (0,0,2) [31], we chose Q positions away from the zone center in order to track the temperature evolution of the inelastic magnon peak. Intriguingly, for (-0.05,-0.05,2) within the in-plane direction (Fig. 2a), no magnon peak is observed at 4 K. Instead, the magnon peak emerges at higher temperatures, with its center exhibiting a nonmonotonic change approaching TC. For (0,0,1.7) in the out-of-plane direction (Fig. 2b), the peak center consistently shifts to lower energies with increasing temperature. To eliminate the influence of the Bose statistics, we correct the raw data with the Bose population factor, and plot them in Fig. 2c,d. We fit these corrected results by convoluting the momentum- and energy-dependent instrumental resolution with a damped harmonic oscillator (DHO) formula, which is applicable to damped spin waves [31, 46–48]. The DHO formula has a form of χ′′(Q,E) ∝ γE E0/[(E2−E02)2+(γE)2], where E0 is the magnon energy and γ is the damping rate (the inverse of γ is proportional to the lifetime of the damped magnons) [31, 46–48]. Based on these DHO fittings in Fig. 2c,d, we can extract the intrinsic damping rate and magnon energy. We emphasize that E0 represents the fitted magnon energy, which does not necessarily coincide with the peak maximum in the measured spectra. This is particularly the case for strongly damped magnons; for example, at 4 K, the peak maximum appears at a much lower energy than E0 (Fig. 2c).

Figure 2e,f presents the extracted γ and E0 plotted as a function of temperature, showcasing the most intriguing results of this work. It is found that for both in-plane and out-of-plane directions, γ shows an upturn toward both 0 K and TC, causing a minimum around T∗d ∼ 90 K. While disorder or vacancies may affect local moments and make spin waves broader, such effect, if present, is more likely to be temperature independent, and therefore would not be responsible for the observed nonmonotonic temperature dependence. On the other hand, this phenomenon is reminiscent of the resistivity minimum caused by the Kondo effect in the original single-impurity Kondo model (Fig. 1d) [1–4], where thermodynamic and transport properties depend logarithmically on temperature as −ln(T) [1–4]. Inspired by this, we use a similar logarithmic term to describe the divergent behaviour toward 0 K. In the meantime, a power-law term describing the spin-wave damping in the hydrodynamic regime is also required to explain the divergence toward TC [49, 50]. Actually, these two effects should exist simultaneously over the entire temperature range below TC. Therefore, the general formula should consist of the linear combination of the two terms, which reads as,

γ(T) = AIn(T∗d/T)+B(1−T/TC)−ν. (1)

To fit the data, we fix T∗d = 90 K and TC = 160 K, and allow A,B,ν to be free. The fitting results well reproduce the unusual nonmonotonic temperature evolution of γ for both in-plane (Fig. 2e) and out-of-plane (Fig. 2f) directions. Specifically, we obtain Ain = 1.617±0.204, Bin = 0.834±0.100, and νin = 0.715±0.087 for the in-plane direction, and Aout = 0.356 ± 0.024, Bout = 0.406 ± 0.025, and νout = 0.490 ± 0.040 for the out-of-plane direction. The distinct parameter values for the in-plane and out-of-plane directions indicate the presence of magnetic anisotropy in this material.

The extracted magnon energy E0 shown in Fig. 2e,f exhibits distinct behaviours for the in- and out-of-plane directions. With increasing temperature, it is found that the out-of-plane E0 softens through a power law while approaching TC (Fig. 2f), a behaviour similar to the temperature evolution of the magnetization in Fe3−xGeTe2 [36, 51]. On the other hand, the in-plane E0 keeps almost constant across T∗d and slightly softens upon cooling to lower temperatures (Fig. 2e). We attribute these two distinct behaviours of E0 to different degrees of Kondo coupling along the two directions. Notably, the magnitude of γ for the in-plane direction is much larger than that for the out-of-plane direction, being approximately four times greater at 4 K. This anisotropy can be explained by the quasi-two-dimensional vdW structure of Fe3−xGeTe2, which promotes a more itinerant electron character in the a-b plane and results in stronger in-plane Kondo coupling. Consequently, the in-plane Kondo screening markedly reduces the intralayer exchange coupling between local moments, leading to the observed decrease in the in-plane E0 at low temperatures (Fig. 2e).

Momentum dependence of the scaling behaviour

To examine whether these behaviours can also be observed in other momenta, we plot the results of the low-energy spin-wave excitations and their damping rate as a function of momentum in Fig. 3. We focus on the excitations at 90 K, where the spin waves are most coherent with the least damping. The energy scans along [110] and [001] directions are plotted in Fig. 3a,d. As Q increases, the peak centers shift gradually to higher energies, accompanied by a broadening of the linewidth and a weakening of the scattering intensities, indicating the nature of damped spin waves. We perform DHO fittings to these scans to extract the momentum dependence of E0 (Fig. 3b,e) and γ (Fig. 3c,f) for the two directions. The dispersions are fitted using the quadratic relation E0 = ∆+DQ2, where ∆ and D are the spin gap and spin-wave stiffness, respectively. The fittings yield D of 54.3±0.8 meV ˚A2 for the [110] direction (Fig. 3b) and 71.2 ± 1.3 meV ˚A2 for the [001] direction (Fig. 3e) at 90 K. For γ, we found a quasi-quadratic dependence (∼ q2.2) in the in-plane direction (Fig. 3c) and a linear dependence in the out-of-plane direction (Fig. 3f).

The low-energy spin waves at other temperatures like 4, 45 and 130 K are also measured. With increasing temperature, we find that the spin-wave dispersion remains nearly unchanged for the in-plane direction but softens considerably for the out-of-plane direction (Fig. 3b,e). Note that since the in-plane spin waves are heavily damped at 4 K, it is challenging to extract a reasonable dispersion. We find that the original q-dependences of γ at 90 K remain applicable at other temperatures, i.e., γ ∼ ηq2.2 and γ ∼ ηq, although the magnitude and coefficient η of the damping vary due to the temperature dependence of the Kondo screening effect (Fig. 3c,f). To further illustrate the temperature evolution of the spin waves, we plot the extracted spin-wave stiffness D and damping coefficient η as a function of temperature in Fig. 3g,h. The out-of-plane D follows a typical power-law relation with temperature, while the in-plane one remains nearly constant. For η, it follows a nonmonotonic dependence and can still be elucidated using Eq. 1 with fixed T∗d = 90 K and TC = 160 K for both directions. Together with Fig. 2e,f, these findings uncover a universal law independent of the momentum governed by the Kondo physics in Fe3−xGeTe2.

FMKH model and spin-flip scattering mechanism

Notably, the temperature at which this damping minimum occurs (Fig. 2e,f and Fig. 3h) is close to the incoherent-coherent crossover observed in the resistivity curve (Fig. 1d). Below the intermediate temperature, the localized electronic state hybridizes with the itinerant electronic state, enlarging the Fermi surface volume and effective electron mass[29]. Consequently, from the perspective of conduction electrons, the slope of resistivity changes (Fig. 1d), consistent with other experimental observations [29–31, 34], manifesting heavy-fermion behaviour. On the other hand, from the perspective of spin waves, these processes provide additional decay channels for magnons, resulting in a significant damping of magnons at low temperatures.

To understand the anomalous magnon damping behaviour microscopically, we develop an FMKH model, considering the dominant role of direct ferromagnetic (FM) exchange interactions between localized d moments and their competition with Kondo coupling in Fe3−xGeTe2 (Methods). The strong direct exchange interactions arise from the spatially extended nature of the outermost 3d orbitals, whose significant overlap stabilizes robust long-range FM order and a relatively high TC. This stands in sharp contrast to conventional f-electron Kondo-lattice systems, where the highly localized f orbitals are effectively screened by conduction electrons and the local f moments couple primarily via weaker, indirect Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interactions, which often favor antiferromagnetic order and yield lower ordering temperatures [8–10, 13, 14]. In Fe3−xGeTe2, the localized d moments are only partially screened by itinerant electrons (Fig. 1b). Within this framework, magnons as collective modes of local moments are interacting with conduction electrons via Kondo coupling [32, 52], giving rise to the Kondo effect [29–31]. To characterize such effect, we employ tensor-network methods to compute the dynamical properties of a minimal 1D FMKH system at finite temperature, represented by a two-leg ladder: one leg as a chain of local moments and the other as itinerant electrons (Fig. 4a) (see Methods for details).

The calculated damping rate for the FM phase of the FMKH model (JK/|JH|=1) is shown in Fig. 4c. A clear damping minimum at T∗d is observed, contrasting with the monotonic behaviour in the pure Heisenberg model (JK/|JH|=0). Notably, our simulations also reveal a logarithmic scaling γ(T) ∼ ln(T0/T) below T∗d. This damping minimum and logarithmic scaling behaviour can be observed in various momenta and for different Kondo couplings in the FM phase (Supplementary Fig. 2), indicating that it is a universal feature arising from the scattering between magnons and itinerant electrons.

We emphasize that the key mechanism underlying the anomalous magnon decay is spin-flip scattering between conduction electrons and magnons induced by the Kondo coupling. In these processes, a magnon decays into a fermionic particle-hole pair, providing an additional channel for damping (Fig. 4a). In the weak-coupling limit (JK ≪ |JH|) relevant to Fe3−xGeTe2 (Fig. 1e), the magnon self-energy is given diagrammatically in Fig. 4(b), where the renormalized vertex plays a critical role in enabling anomalous magnon decay [53]. In sharp contrast to the usual vertex correction due to electron-phonon coupling—which is negligible due to Migdal theorem [54] — here the vertex correction of JK in Fig. 4b is crucial at low temperatures. By applying the renormalization of the Kondo coupling, formally similar to the single-impurity Kondo problem but here used to describe the momentum-dependent renormalization and damping of magnons, a log(1/T)-like temperature dependence of the magnon self-energy can be obtained. Furthermore, as the kinematically allowed phase space for magnon-electron scattering increases with increasing magnon momentum Q (See Supplementary Fig. 4), the magnon damping becomes stronger with Q at low temperatures, in agreement with the experimental observations in Fig. 3.
paper_content.methods:
Crystal growth and INS experiments. High-quality single crystals of Fe3−xGeTe2 were grown using self-flux method, as described in Refs. 31, 63. This growth method naturally introduces Fe vacancies, which reduce both the Curie temperature and the saturation magnetization. To make sure that different pieces of single crystals had the same amount of Fe vacancies, we measured the magnetization on four randomly picked single crystals from different growth batches. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, they have nearly identical susceptibility curves with a single TC ∼ 160 K, regardless the growth batch. This is in good agreement with our prior magnetization and resistivity measurements, as well as with the temperature evolution of the magnetic Bragg peak (Ref. 31). These results confirm the homogeneity of the crystals used in this study. The INS experiments were performed on Sika, a cold-neutron triple-axis spectrometer located at the OPAL facility of ANSTO in Australia [64, 65]. The Fe3−xGeTe2 sample array used in the measurements was the same as that employed in Ref. 31. It was composed of well coaligned single crystals with a mosaic of 1.6◦ within the a-b plane and 1.7◦ along the c axis (Supplementary Fig. 5), and mounted in the (H, H, L) scattering plane. Measurements were carried out using a fixed final-energy mode with Ef = 5.0 meV, where both incident and final neutron energies were determined by pyrolytic graphite (002) crystals. Double and vertical focusing modes were applied for the monochromator and analyzer, respectively. A cooled Be filter was placed after the sample during the first experimental run (corresponding to Fig. 2) and removed in the subsequent run, resulting in higher detected neutron intensity (corresponding to Fig. 3). An open-open-60′-60′ collimation was used to strike a fine balance between neutron flux and experimental resolution. These settings gave an energy resolution of ∼ 0.2 meV at the elastic line. To ensure sufficient statistics, each inelastic data point was counted for ∼ 5 minutes. Throughout the paper, the wavevector Q is expressed as (H, K, L) in reciprocal lattice unit (r.l.u.) of (a∗, b∗, c∗) = (4π/√3a, 4π/√3b, 2π/c) with refined lattice parameters a = b = 3.946 ˚A and c = 16.357 ˚A in a hexagonal structure.

FMKH model and tensor-network calculations. The FMKH model considered in this work reads

H = −t ∑n,σ (c†n+1,σ cn,σ +H.c.) + JH ∑n S n ·S n+1 + JK ∑n S n ·s n, (2)

where c†n,σ (cn,σ) is the creation (annihilation) operator of the conduction electron at site n with spin σ ∈ {↑,↓}, and S n (s n) represents the spin operator of local moment (conduction electron). The finite-temperature dynamical properties of this model are calculated by the tensor-network methods (for 1D chain) [40–45], and analyzed by perturbative calculations (also for higher dimensions [62]). The tensor-network calculation process can be divided into two parts: first, obtaining the equilibrium thermal density matrix, and second, performing real-time evolution on that density matrix. The equilibrium thermal density matrix and related thermodynamic properties can be obtained by the matrix product operator (MPO) based tensor-network methods [40–42]. Given the MPO representation of the thermal density matrix, we generalize the tangent-space approach for real-time evolution [43–45] to the mixed states and study the temperature evolution of the spectral density.

In the calculations, FM coupling strength JH = −1 is taken as the energy unit and the hopping energy is set as t/|JH| = 2 throughout the calculations. The simulations are restricted within the 2-leg ladder structure of size N = L×2 with the length L = 16. This moderate system size is chosen so as to guarantee converged dynamical data at finite temperature. One chain comprises local moments, while the other represents itinerant electrons. These two chains are coupled through Kondo interactions. The retained bond dimension is D = 1600, which guarantees accurate results till low temperature T/|JH| ≃ 0.01. Given the MPO representation of the thermal density matrix ρ(β) = e−βH (β ≡ 1/T), the dynamical properties at temperature T can be simulated through a successive real-time evolution. The spectral function χ′′(Q,E) ≈ − ∫tmax0 dt Im [g(Q,t)]sin(Et) · W(t/tmax) is of central interest in studying the dynamical properties at finite temperature, where W is the Hanning window function, t is the evolution time, and the (dynamical) correlation function is g(Q,t) = ⟨A Q(t)A† Q⟩ β, with A Q = √ 1/L ∑n S n+eiQn being the Fourier transformed spin operator. The time-dependent correlation function g(Q,t) can be obtained by tangent-space approach [43–45]. In the real-time evolution calculations, we consider a 16×2 lattice and evolution time up to tmax = 20/|JH|, with D = 4800 bond states retained. The damping rate γ is obtained through the DHO fitting of numerical results (see more details in Supplementary Information).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript presents a detailed experimental investigation of the temperature evolution of magnon damping in the van der Waals metallic ferromagnet Fe3-xGeTe2. Using inelastic neutron scattering, the authors observe a nonmonotonic temperature dependence of the magnon linewidth, characterized by a minimum at an intermediate temperature (~90 K), with increased damping both at low and high temperatures. This behavior is attributed to the interplay between thermal fluctuations and Kondo screening.
While the experimental data are of good quality, the results appear incremental in the context of extensive prior studies on this material. The key observation, nonmonotonic magnon damping, may be of interest, but it does not in itself constitute a conceptual advance sufficient for publication in a high-impact journal. Similar nonmonotonic behavior of the magnetic relaxation rate has been reported in heavy-fermion compounds as early as the 1980s. For example, Z. Phys. B 77, 95–104 (1989) and J. Magn. Magn. Mater. 74, 341–346 (1988) documented comparable temperature dependencies in Ce-based Kondo lattices. Theoretical interpretations of such behavior were also developed, including in J. Appl. Phys. 57, 3166–3168 (1985) and Phys. Rev. Lett. 54, 230–233 (1985). These precedents are not cited or discussed. If the intended contribution is to provide further evidence of Kondo physics in a 3d-electron system, this point has already been well established through multiple experimental techniques and in prior work by the same group. The manuscript does not make sufficiently clear what genuinely new insight is gained here.
The comparison with the FMKH model is, in my view, fundamentally flawed and overly simplistic. The model lacks direct relevance to the real material, which is a quasi-2D lattice system with multi-orbital degrees of freedom. The minimal 1D model presented here at best can serve as an illustration. It is unjustified to support a quantitative or qualitative comparison with experimental data. If the authors wish to pursue this model further, it would be more appropriate to present those results in a separate work, as has already been done in Ref. 56.
The choice of in-plane momentum transfer confuses me. Why did the authors choose an offset position like (−0.05, −0.05, 2) rather than the zone center at (0, 0, 2)? Is the magnon spectrum gapped at all temperatures?
The green data in panel 2c appear to correspond to the same scan shown in panel 3a. Why do the intensity not match?
In summary, I believe the results could be appropriate for publication in a more specialized journal focused on magnetism or neutron scattering, but do not currently meet the threshold for a high-impact journal.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this work, the authors explore the temperature-dependent behavior of magnon damping in ferromagnetic van der Waals (vdW) metal Fe3-xGeTe2, unveiling significant mechanisms underlying the interaction between ferromagnetism and the Kondo effect. Due to interactions between localized spins from the magnetic ions and the conduction electrons, the Kondo effect enhances electron-magnon scattering at lower temperatures with a logarithmic temperature dependence resistance, which transfers the spin angular momentum to increase the damping of the magnon. Thermal fluctuationsthermal fluctuations contribute to dephasing at higher temperatures, and the resistivity follows a power-law. The behavior of itinerant d electrons scattering collective magnon excitations of local moments discussed here has profound implications for the competition between Kondo screening and ferromagnetic exchange interactions. The intricate interplay suggests that the Kondo effect is strong enough to enhance electron-magnon scattering despite the ferromagnetic order below the Kondo temperature TK, which is crucial for developing advanced spintronics such as memory devices and magnetic applications.
In the study, the inelastic neutron scattering (INS) techniques were employed to investigate the low-energy spin waves in Fe3-xGeTe2. The observed phenomena indicate that magnon damping diverges at both low and high temperatures while demonstrating a distinct minimum at an intermediate temperature. Exploring the magnon dynamics in metallic van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnets Fe3-xGeTe2 allows for the meticulous examination of temperature-driven changes in spin wave behavior. Traditionally examined in f-electron systems (like those involving Ce or Yb ions), the Kondo effect is also critical in d-electron systems where localized d-orbital electrons interact with the conduction sea. The Kondo effect intricately alters the material's transport properties, such as electrical resistivity and thermopower. Upon cooling below $ T_C \approx 160 $ K, the magnon damping rate $ Gamma$ initially decreases, reaching a minimum at approximately $ T^* \approx 90 $ K. This behavior indicates reduced magnon-magnon and magnon-electron scattering in this temperature range. When Kondo interactions dominate, the magnetic moments are screened, leading to a non-magnetic ground state. The mechanism intertwining Kondo coupling and magnetic interactions in d-electron systems involves both direct exchange and indirect interactions mediated by conduction electrons. Tensor-Network Techniques model quantum many-body systems by efficiently capturing entanglement and dynamic interactions. Simulations reproduced the damping minimum and logarithmic temperature scaling, validating the accuracy of ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg (FMKH) model in describing electron-magnon interactions and spin dynamics. This method reveals underlying phenomena of magnon damping and its distinctive temperature dependency.
Overall, I would like to consider to recommend its publication in Nature Communications which has high standards and requirements if the following questions can be answered clearly and correctly, including the resistivity behavior, temperature-dependent magnon damping, and the implications of electron-magnon scattering linked to Kondo effect.
1. The authors say "These results shed light on the interplay between spin exchange and Kondo coupling in metallic 3d-electron systems with magnetic order, ... " Although d-electrons are more delocalized compared to f-electrons, localized d-orbital electrons can still interact with conduction electrons to form localized moments strong enough for the Kondo effect. But how exactly direct exchange plays into the Kondo mechanism? Direct exchange between d-electrons and conduction electrons? Or direct exchange between localized d-moments?
2. In the introduction it reads "The van der Waals (vdW) metallic ferromagnet Fe3-xGeTe2 is one such example material." Considering the role of the van der Waals nature in layered material, in-plane conduction electrons interact more strongly with localized moments than out-of-plane. How does this anisotropy affects magnetic properties of Fe3-xGeTe2? Wether the in-plane conductivity enhance different damping along different crystallographic directions?
3. In Fig. 1, when considering the canonical Doniach phase diagram for a ferromagnetic Kondo lattice, how to demonstrates the competition between Kondo and ordering? And how does that tie into the Kondo effect?
4. In the Introduction the authors claim that ‘this resistivity behaviour aligns with observations in other d-electron systems exhibiting a heavy-fermion state’. Unlike 4f-electron systems, 3d electrons are more itinerant, which could affect the combined effects of Heisenberg exchange and Kondo interactions, how they compete or coexist? And Fe3-xGeTe2 has some stoichiometric variation, so the static disorder like vacancies or site substitutions becomes more impactful at lower temperatures. What about the role of disorder?
5. The moments are more isolated in f-systems, so the interactions are purely via conduction electrons, while there are more direct exchange between neighboring d-orbitals, complicating the picture. The Kondo effect in d-electron systems involves both the Hund's coupling within the d-orbitals and the RKKY mediated by conduction electrons. Since crystal fields can split d-orbitals, how do crystal field effects influence this?
6. As they mentioned the $gamma$ increases again below Td* due to the magnon-phonon interactions and new scattering channels. At lower temperatures, phonon populations decrease since phonons are thermal vibrations, wouldn't that reduce magnon-phonon scattering? If certain phonon modes are no longer thermally excited, the remaining phonons could have wavelengths that couple more effectively with magnons. The increase in damping below Td* might be due to the freezing out of some degrees of freedom. Whether the lattice parameters change with temperature, affecting the overlap between magnon and phonon modes? And why the optimal condition for magnon modes is around 90 K?
7. They reproduced observed phenomena in the magnon damping minimum and logarithmic scaling within a ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg (FMKH) model. This sophisticated approach leverages tensor-network techniques to accurately capture the complex interactions in quantum many-body systems. The logarithmic term is dominant at low temperatures, illustrating the enhanced Kondo screening effect, where localized magnetic moments interact strongly with conduction electrons, reducing magnetic scattering. The power-law term becomes significant at higher temperatures, reflecting the thermal excitation's impact on the resistivity.
The logarithmic scaling mentioned emerges from the interplay between the Kondo effect and ferromagnetism with specific temperature dependencies in the damping rate. They reproduced magnon damping minimum and a logarithmic scaling using tensor-network simulations. And how does the iron-deficiency in Fe3-xGeTe2 affect the Kondo effect and the Heisenberg interactions? What about the probably influences of the magnetic properties, like changing the number of localized spins or altering the conduction electron density?
8.In page 7, The authors write "This model consists of both itinerant electrons and local moments, reflecting the dual nature of d-orbital magnetism in the compound." The itinerant d electrons are interacting with the magnons through spin-flip processes, which is subject to renormalization effects analogous to those in the single-impurity Kondo problem. Considering the interplay between spin dynamics of itinerant electrons and collective magnetic excitations mediated by Kondo interactions, how the collective nature of magnons alters the scattering compared to single impurity cases? Does the exact mechanism of renormalization in this context involve more complex many-body effects than the traditional Kondo model?
9. They suggest optimal conditions where thermal fluctuations are subdued, and magnon modes are relatively undisturbed by scattering processes. Around Td* $\sim$ 90 K, the magnon damping rate is minimized. Below Td*, the damping rate rapidly increases again, likely due to enhanced magnon-phonon interactions and the onset of new scattering channels as the temperature approaches the low-temperature regime. Dominant near and above Td*, these interactions lead to damping reduction as cooperative magnetic ordering stabilizes. Below Td*, increased lattice vibrations contribute to enhanced magnon-phonon scattering, resulting in higher damping rates. Initial damping rate decrease aligns with reduced thermal disturbance and stable magnon propagation. The crossover near Td* marks a balance point between magnon scattering suppression and the potential onset of complex interactions. The minimum damping rate reflects an equilibrium state where magnon interactions are minimized. The Kondo effect itself has a characteristic temperature scale (Kondo temperature), how electron-magnon interactions fit in the heavy fermion systems? How renormalization shapes the balance between scattering mechanisms at different temperature regimes?
10. Metallic ferromagnets have itinerant electrons, so the damping might be related to Stoner excitations, where electron-hole pairs are created, affecting the magnons. But as temperature increases towards the Curie temperature, the magnetic order starts to weaken, leading to more thermal fluctuations and thus more damping. Thus, how to address the magnon overdamping or the spectrum softening?
11. In Eq. (2), the authors couple Kondo screening and magnetic ordering in d-electron systems involves spin-orbit coupling typically. reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript detail an experimental study of spin waves in Fe deficient Fe3-xGeTe2 compound using inelastic neutron scattering. The experiments are complemented by numerical simulations. The authors claim to have found anomalous increase in the damping of the magnons at both high and low temperatures, displaying a minima at about 90 K, and relate this to the Kondo coupling in magnetically ordered systems. I do find this investigation of scientific interest, however, in my opinion, the findings in themselves are not impactful enough to warrant publication in Nature Communications. I would instead suggest to pursue publication in a more specialized journal. In addition, I have some concerns about the data analysis and interpretation, as detailed below, which give me some doubt about the robustness of the presented (key) results.
The inelastic neutron scattering (INS) study is conducted using a cold-neutron triple-axis instrument. For the type of detailed analysis and interpretation presented in this manuscript, I would definitely expect the authors to conduct a complete and thorough resolution analysis/deconvolution (resolution ellipsoid for a TAS instrument). This is especially important for the Q-dependent data-set AND because the c-axis of this sample is so large (i.e. small c*). It is also vital to know the “vertical acceptance/resolution” for the instrument. Here any “contamination” from the resolution ellipsoid touching the base of any nuclear Bragg peaks can easily affect the width of the magnon peak (i.e. the lifetime/damping). There is also no information about the sample mosaic, i.e. how well aligned are the collection of samples (the mosaicity of the total sample used in the INS experiments). Some scans about this should also be shown in the supplementary material in order to verify that the presented effect does not come from contamination of signal from nuclear Bragg or other magnetic intensities.
I also have some questions regarding the analysis/results. In my understanding, the E0 parameter that is plotted e.g. in Fig. 2(e,f), is simply the peak center for the magnon. In this case, looking e.g. at the actual data of Fig. 2(c) and comparing it to results in Fig. 2(e), it does not seem to match. For instance, the blue 4 K data shows a peak center around 0.3 meV in Fig. 2(c), however, in Fig. 2(e) the blue point at 4 K is around 1 meV. Further, in Fig. 2(e) there is a blue point at Tc however, no red point is shown, but the red line indicate that there might be a point very high up (outside the graph). In fact, the main point indicating that there is a strong increase in the damping for higher temperatures is the 140 K point in Fig. 2(e). However, looking at the actual fits in Fig. 2(c), for me it is not evident that this peak is much broader than the green 90 K data. Finally, the 4 K peak in Fig. 2(c) should according to plot in Fig. 2(e) be broader than all other peaks... it definitely does not look like this is the case (which also matches the fact that center E0 seems to be wrong). All these points makes me partly doubt the final presented (key) results about divergence of magnon damping at both high and low temperature.
Finally, I would have liked to see some information about the sample quality also in this manuscript (and/or supplementary material). It would be of vital importance to show that this Fe deficient sample is not phase separated. I also did not find any information about this in Reference 31 (which present data from the same sample).
In summary, I cannot recommend publication of the current manuscript in Nature Communications.

## Abstract

In d-electron systems, there can also be intricate interplay between Kondo coupling and magnetic interactions as that in f-electron systems, but the underlying mechanism remains elusive. Here, using inelastic neutron scattering, we investigate the temperature evolution of the low-energy spin waves (magnons) in a metallic van der Waals ferromagnet Fe3−xGeTe2, and observe that the magnon damping diverges at both low and high temperatures and exhibits a minimum at an intermediate temperature. These behaviours are described by a formula that combines logarithmic and power-law terms, representing the dominant contributions from Kondo coupling and thermal fluctuations, respectively. These findings can be explained by considering electron-magnon scattering of spin-flip type within the ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg lattice model, distinct from the original Kondo effect which only considers the coupling between itinerant electrons and isolated impurity spins. These results unveil the intriguing interplay between itinerant electrons and spin waves in metallic 3d-electron systems with magnetic order, and provide magnon damping as a new effective probe of Kondo coupling in metallic quantum magnets, thereby opening new avenues for exploring Kondo physics from the magnon perspective.

---

## Introduction

The original Kondo effect in dilute magnetic alloys, which takes the resistivity minimum as one of the characteristics, describes the scattering of conduction electrons by magnetic impurities in such systems [1, 2]. This effect is classified as the single-impurity Kondo problem and is now well understood based on the spin-flip scatterings of conduction electrons off the single-impurity spins (Fig. 1a) [1, 2]. The concept of Kondo physics has been extended to include the correlated electron systems, specifically those consisting of a dense periodic array of local moments interacting with the conduction electron sea through an antiferromagnetic Kondo interaction, referred to as a Kondo lattice (Fig. 1b-d) [2–5]. The Kondo-lattice model was initially proposed to describe the heavy-fermion state in f-electron systems, particularly in intermetallics containing Ce, Yb, or U elements [2–7]. The competition between the Kondo effect and couplings of localized spins underlies various intriguing phenomena in these heavy-fermion compounds (Fig. 1e), including quantum criticality [8–11], strange-metal behaviour [11, 12], magnetism [13–16] and superconductivity[17, 18], which can be tuned by chemical doping, magnetic field or pressure [8–12]. In the strong Kondo coupling regime, the hybridization between localized f electrons and conduction electrons leads to the quenching of local moments and the expansion of the Fermi surface, resulting in the formation of a heavy Fermi-liquid state (Fig. 1c,d) [2–7, 19, 20]. Magnetic order can arise when the strength of the effective magnetic interaction between localized spins exceeds the Kondo coupling. Moreover, the coexistence of magnetic order with Kondo effect [13–16] or superconductivity [17, 18] can be observed, particularly in systems where the duality of f electrons emerges due to the mixed-valence situation and the multiorbital nature [13–18].

More recently, the unexpected heavy-fermion state has also been observed in certain d-electron transition metals, which reside in the intermediate regime between itineracy and localization of d electrons [21–31]. Understanding magnetism within the framework of this duality and the applicability of the Kondo-lattice model to such systems are currently active topics of research [21, 23, 25–31]. The van der Waals (vdW) metallic ferromagnet Fe3−xGeTe2 is one such example material [29–35]. Due to the coexistence of localized and itinerant 3d electrons, there are conflicting reports regarding the microscopic origin of the magnetism in Fe3−xGeTe2 [29–32, 36–39]. In our earlier work, we have reconciled the debate by showing that the ferromagnetism has a dual origin, with local moments and itinerant electrons contributing to the low-energy spin waves and columnlike continua, respectively [31]. Moreover, there is accumulating evidence for the Kondo coupling between these two components, such as the Fano resonance feature [29, 30], large effective electron mass [29, 34, 37], and the incoherent-coherent crossover in transport and magnetic measurements [29]. In particular, the resistivity curve of Fe3−xGeTe2 reveals a slope change at a characteristic temperature of approximately 90 K, as depicted in Fig. 1d. Below this temperature, the Kondo-lattice behaviour emerges in the magnetic ordering phase, accompanied by the enhancement of Fermi surface volume and effective electron mass [29]. Notably, this resistivity behaviour aligns with observations in other d-electron systems exhibiting a heavy-fermion state [22, 24, 25], but is distinct from either the Kondo-impurity model or the Kondo lattice in f-electron systems (Fig. 1d). Since our earlier work has indicated that Kondo screening significantly enhances spin-wave damping at 4 K compared to 100 K [31], a question naturally arises: will the damping follow certain scaling behaviour due to the Kondo coupling effect?

Here we report inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements on the temperature evolution of low-energy spin waves in Fe-deficient Fe3−xGeTe2 single crystals with Curie temperature TC ∼ 160 K. Upon cooling from TC, we observe that the magnon damping rate initially decreases, reaching a minimum around T∗d ∼ 90 K, before rapidly increasing again. This behaviour follows a scaling relation combining both logarithmic and power-law terms. Additionally, we find that the in-plane Kondo coupling is stronger than the out-of-plane coupling, resulting in a softening of in-plane magnons at low temperatures. Using the state-of-the-art tensor-network algorithm [40–45], we reproduce the observed magnon damping minimum and logarithmic scaling within a ferromagnetic Kondo-Heisenberg (FMKH) model. Although the form is analogous to the original Kondo effect describing the coupling between itinerant electrons and impurity spins [1, 2], the underlying mechanism is essentially different — here, itinerant d electrons scatter the collective excitations of local moments via a spin-flip process induced by Kondo coupling. Our results provide compelling evidence for the existence of Kondo effect in the metallic ferromagnet Fe3−xGeTe2, and demonstrate magnon damping as an effective probe for the Kondo coupling in systems where magnetic order and Kondo effect coexist.

## Results

Damping rate minimum and logarithmic scaling

Figure 2a,b shows the energy scans at various temperatures for the off-centered in-plane and out-of-plane positions, respectively. As no sizable spin gap was observed at the zone center (0,0,2) [31], we chose Q positions away from the zone center in order to track the temperature evolution of the inelastic magnon peak. Intriguingly, for (-0.05,-0.05,2) within the in-plane direction (Fig. 2a), no magnon peak is observed at 4 K. Instead, the magnon peak emerges at higher temperatures, with its center exhibiting a nonmonotonic change approaching TC. For (0,0,1.7) in the out-of-plane direction (Fig. 2b), the peak center consistently shifts to lower energies with increasing temperature. To eliminate the influence of the Bose statistics, we correct the raw data with the Bose population factor, and plot them in Fig. 2c,d. We fit these corrected results by convoluting the momentum- and energy-dependent instrumental resolution with a damped harmonic oscillator (DHO) formula, which is applicable to damped spin waves [31, 46–48]. The DHO formula has a form of χ′′(Q,E) ∝ γE E0/[(E2−E02)2+(γE)2], where E0 is the magnon energy and γ is the damping rate (the inverse of γ is proportional to the lifetime of the damped magnons) [31, 46–48]. Based on these DHO fittings in Fig. 2c,d, we can extract the intrinsic damping rate and magnon energy. We emphasize that E0 represents the fitted magnon energy, which does not necessarily coincide with the peak maximum in the measured spectra. This is particularly the case for strongly damped magnons; for example, at 4 K, the peak maximum appears at a much lower energy than E0 (Fig. 2c).

Figure 2e,f presents the extracted γ and E0 plotted as a function of temperature, showcasing the most intriguing results of this work. It is found that for both in-plane and out-of-plane directions, γ shows an upturn toward both 0 K and TC, causing a minimum around T∗d ∼ 90 K. While disorder or vacancies may affect local moments and make spin waves broader, such effect, if present, is more likely to be temperature independent, and therefore would not be responsible for the observed nonmonotonic temperature dependence. On the other hand, this phenomenon is reminiscent of the resistivity minimum caused by the Kondo effect in the original single-impurity Kondo model (Fig. 1d) [1–4], where thermodynamic and transport properties depend logarithmically on temperature as −ln(T) [1–4]. Inspired by this, we use a similar logarithmic term to describe the divergent behaviour toward 0 K. In the meantime, a power-law term describing the spin-wave damping in the hydrodynamic regime is also required to explain the divergence toward TC [49, 50]. Actually, these two effects should exist simultaneously over the entire temperature range below TC. Therefore, the general formula should consist of the linear combination of the two terms, which reads as,

γ(T) = AIn(T∗d/T)+B(1−T/TC)−ν. (1)

To fit the data, we fix T∗d = 90 K and TC = 160 K, and allow A,B,ν to be free. The fitting results well reproduce the unusual nonmonotonic temperature evolution of γ for both in-plane (Fig. 2e) and out-of-plane (Fig. 2f) directions. Specifically, we obtain Ain = 1.617±0.204, Bin = 0.834±0.100, and νin = 0.715±0.087 for the in-plane direction, and Aout = 0.356 ± 0.024, Bout = 0.406 ± 0.025, and νout = 0.490 ± 0.040 for the out-of-plane direction. The distinct parameter values for the in-plane and out-of-plane directions indicate the presence of magnetic anisotropy in this material.

The extracted magnon energy E0 shown in Fig. 2e,f exhibits distinct behaviours for the in- and out-of-plane directions. With increasing temperature, it is found that the out-of-plane E0 softens through a power law while approaching TC (Fig. 2f), a behaviour similar to the temperature evolution of the magnetization in Fe3−xGeTe2 [36, 51]. On the other hand, the in-plane E0 keeps almost constant across T∗d and slightly softens upon cooling to lower temperatures (Fig. 2e). We attribute these two distinct behaviours of E0 to different degrees of Kondo coupling along the two directions. Notably, the magnitude of γ for the in-plane direction is much larger than that for the out-of-plane direction, being approximately four times greater at 4 K. This anisotropy can be explained by the quasi-two-dimensional vdW structure of Fe3−xGeTe2, which promotes a more itinerant electron character in the a-b plane and results in stronger in-plane Kondo coupling. Consequently, the in-plane Kondo screening markedly reduces the intralayer exchange coupling between local moments, leading to the observed decrease in the in-plane E0 at low temperatures (Fig. 2e).

Momentum dependence of the scaling behaviour

To examine whether these behaviours can also be observed in other momenta, we plot the results of the low-energy spin-wave excitations and their damping rate as a function of momentum in Fig. 3. We focus on the excitations at 90 K, where the spin waves are most coherent with the least damping. The energy scans along [110] and [001] directions are plotted in Fig. 3a,d. As Q increases, the peak centers shift gradually to higher energies, accompanied by a broadening of the linewidth and a weakening of the scattering intensities, indicating the nature of damped spin waves. We perform DHO fittings to these scans to extract the momentum dependence of E0 (Fig. 3b,e) and γ (Fig. 3c,f) for the two directions. The dispersions are fitted using the quadratic relation E0 = ∆+DQ2, where ∆ and D are the spin gap and spin-wave stiffness, respectively. The fittings yield D of 54.3±0.8 meV ˚A2 for the [110] direction (Fig. 3b) and 71.2 ± 1.3 meV ˚A2 for the [001] direction (Fig. 3e) at 90 K. For γ, we found a quasi-quadratic dependence (∼ q2.2) in the in-plane direction (Fig. 3c) and a linear dependence in the out-of-plane direction (Fig. 3f).

The low-energy spin waves at other temperatures like 4, 45 and 130 K are also measured. With increasing temperature, we find that the spin-wave dispersion remains nearly unchanged for the in-plane direction but softens considerably for the out-of-plane direction (Fig. 3b,e). Note that since the in-plane spin waves are heavily damped at 4 K, it is challenging to extract a reasonable dispersion. We find that the original q-dependences of γ at 90 K remain applicable at other temperatures, i.e., γ ∼ ηq2.2 and γ ∼ ηq, although the magnitude and coefficient η of the damping vary due to the temperature dependence of the Kondo screening effect (Fig. 3c,f). To further illustrate the temperature evolution of the spin waves, we plot the extracted spin-wave stiffness D and damping coefficient η as a function of temperature in Fig. 3g,h. The out-of-plane D follows a typical power-law relation with temperature, while the in-plane one remains nearly constant. For η, it follows a nonmonotonic dependence and can still be elucidated using Eq. 1 with fixed T∗d = 90 K and TC = 160 K for both directions. Together with Fig. 2e,f, these findings uncover a universal law independent of the momentum governed by the Kondo physics in Fe3−xGeTe2.

FMKH model and spin-flip scattering mechanism

Notably, the temperature at which this damping minimum occurs (Fig. 2e,f and Fig. 3h) is close to the incoherent-coherent crossover observed in the resistivity curve (Fig. 1d). Below the intermediate temperature, the localized electronic state hybridizes with the itinerant electronic state, enlarging the Fermi surface volume and effective electron mass[29]. Consequently, from the perspective of conduction electrons, the slope of resistivity changes (Fig. 1d), consistent with other experimental observations [29–31, 34], manifesting heavy-fermion behaviour. On the other hand, from the perspective of spin waves, these processes provide additional decay channels for magnons, resulting in a significant damping of magnons at low temperatures.

To understand the anomalous magnon damping behaviour microscopically, we develop an FMKH model, considering the dominant role of direct ferromagnetic (FM) exchange interactions between localized d moments and their competition with Kondo coupling in Fe3−xGeTe2 (Methods). The strong direct exchange interactions arise from the spatially extended nature of the outermost 3d orbitals, whose significant overlap stabilizes robust long-range FM order and a relatively high TC. This stands in sharp contrast to conventional f-electron Kondo-lattice systems, where the highly localized f orbitals are effectively screened by conduction electrons and the local f moments couple primarily via weaker, indirect Ruderman-Kittel-Kasuya-Yosida (RKKY) interactions, which often favor antiferromagnetic order and yield lower ordering temperatures [8–10, 13, 14]. In Fe3−xGeTe2, the localized d moments are only partially screened by itinerant electrons (Fig. 1b). Within this framework, magnons as collective modes of local moments are interacting with conduction electrons via Kondo coupling [32, 52], giving rise to the Kondo effect [29–31]. To characterize such effect, we employ tensor-network methods to compute the dynamical properties of a minimal 1D FMKH system at finite temperature, represented by a two-leg ladder: one leg as a chain of local moments and the other as itinerant electrons (Fig. 4a) (see Methods for details).

The calculated damping rate for the FM phase of the FMKH model (JK/|JH|=1) is shown in Fig. 4c. A clear damping minimum at T∗d is observed, contrasting with the monotonic behaviour in the pure Heisenberg model (JK/|JH|=0). Notably, our simulations also reveal a logarithmic scaling γ(T) ∼ ln(T0/T) below T∗d. This damping minimum and logarithmic scaling behaviour can be observed in various momenta and for different Kondo couplings in the FM phase (Supplementary Fig. 2), indicating that it is a universal feature arising from the scattering between magnons and itinerant electrons.

We emphasize that the key mechanism underlying the anomalous magnon decay is spin-flip scattering between conduction electrons and magnons induced by the Kondo coupling. In these processes, a magnon decays into a fermionic particle-hole pair, providing an additional channel for damping (Fig. 4a). In the weak-coupling limit (JK ≪ |JH|) relevant to Fe3−xGeTe2 (Fig. 1e), the magnon self-energy is given diagrammatically in Fig. 4(b), where the renormalized vertex plays a critical role in enabling anomalous magnon decay [53]. In sharp contrast to the usual vertex correction due to electron-phonon coupling—which is negligible due to Migdal theorem [54] — here the vertex correction of JK in Fig. 4b is crucial at low temperatures. By applying the renormalization of the Kondo coupling, formally similar to the single-impurity Kondo problem but here used to describe the momentum-dependent renormalization and damping of magnons, a log(1/T)-like temperature dependence of the magnon self-energy can be obtained. Furthermore, as the kinematically allowed phase space for magnon-electron scattering increases with increasing magnon momentum Q (See Supplementary Fig. 4), the magnon damping becomes stronger with Q at low temperatures, in agreement with the experimental observations in Fig. 3.

---

## Methods

Crystal growth and INS experiments. High-quality single crystals of Fe3−xGeTe2 were grown using self-flux method, as described in Refs. 31, 63. This growth method naturally introduces Fe vacancies, which reduce both the Curie temperature and the saturation magnetization. To make sure that different pieces of single crystals had the same amount of Fe vacancies, we measured the magnetization on four randomly picked single crystals from different growth batches. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, they have nearly identical susceptibility curves with a single TC ∼ 160 K, regardless the growth batch. This is in good agreement with our prior magnetization and resistivity measurements, as well as with the temperature evolution of the magnetic Bragg peak (Ref. 31). These results confirm the homogeneity of the crystals used in this study. The INS experiments were performed on Sika, a cold-neutron triple-axis spectrometer located at the OPAL facility of ANSTO in Australia [64, 65]. The Fe3−xGeTe2 sample array used in the measurements was the same as that employed in Ref. 31. It was composed of well coaligned single crystals with a mosaic of 1.6◦ within the a-b plane and 1.7◦ along the c axis (Supplementary Fig. 5), and mounted in the (H, H, L) scattering plane. Measurements were carried out using a fixed final-energy mode with Ef = 5.0 meV, where both incident and final neutron energies were determined by pyrolytic graphite (002) crystals. Double and vertical focusing modes were applied for the monochromator and analyzer, respectively. A cooled Be filter was placed after the sample during the first experimental run (corresponding to Fig. 2) and removed in the subsequent run, resulting in higher detected neutron intensity (corresponding to Fig. 3). An open-open-60′-60′ collimation was used to strike a fine balance between neutron flux and experimental resolution. These settings gave an energy resolution of ∼ 0.2 meV at the elastic line. To ensure sufficient statistics, each inelastic data point was counted for ∼ 5 minutes. Throughout the paper, the wavevector Q is expressed as (H, K, L) in reciprocal lattice unit (r.l.u.) of (a∗, b∗, c∗) = (4π/√3a, 4π/√3b, 2π/c) with refined lattice parameters a = b = 3.946 ˚A and c = 16.357 ˚A in a hexagonal structure.

FMKH model and tensor-network calculations. The FMKH model considered in this work reads

H = −t ∑n,σ (c†n+1,σ cn,σ +H.c.) + JH ∑n S n ·S n+1 + JK ∑n S n ·s n, (2)

where c†n,σ (cn,σ) is the creation (annihilation) operator of the conduction electron at site n with spin σ ∈ {↑,↓}, and S n (s n) represents the spin operator of local moment (conduction electron). The finite-temperature dynamical properties of this model are calculated by the tensor-network methods (for 1D chain) [40–45], and analyzed by perturbative calculations (also for higher dimensions [62]). The tensor-network calculation process can be divided into two parts: first, obtaining the equilibrium thermal density matrix, and second, performing real-time evolution on that density matrix. The equilibrium thermal density matrix and related thermodynamic properties can be obtained by the matrix product operator (MPO) based tensor-network methods [40–42]. Given the MPO representation of the thermal density matrix, we generalize the tangent-space approach for real-time evolution [43–45] to the mixed states and study the temperature evolution of the spectral density.

In the calculations, FM coupling strength JH = −1 is taken as the energy unit and the hopping energy is set as t/|JH| = 2 throughout the calculations. The simulations are restricted within the 2-leg ladder structure of size N = L×2 with the length L = 16. This moderate system size is chosen so as to guarantee converged dynamical data at finite temperature. One chain comprises local moments, while the other represents itinerant electrons. These two chains are coupled through Kondo interactions. The retained bond dimension is D = 1600, which guarantees accurate results till low temperature T/|JH| ≃ 0.01. Given the MPO representation of the thermal density matrix ρ(β) = e−βH (β ≡ 1/T), the dynamical properties at temperature T can be simulated through a successive real-time evolution. The spectral function χ′′(Q,E) ≈ − ∫tmax0 dt Im [g(Q,t)]sin(Et) · W(t/tmax) is of central interest in studying the dynamical properties at finite temperature, where W is the Hanning window function, t is the evolution time, and the (dynamical) correlation function is g(Q,t) = ⟨A Q(t)A† Q⟩ β, with A Q = √ 1/L ∑n S n+eiQn being the Fourier transformed spin operator. The time-dependent correlation function g(Q,t) can be obtained by tangent-space approach [43–45]. In the real-time evolution calculations, we consider a 16×2 lattice and evolution time up to tmax = 20/|JH|, with D = 4800 bond states retained. The damping rate γ is obtained through the DHO fitting of numerical results (see more details in Supplementary Information).

In summary, I cannot recommend publication of the current manuscript in Nature Communications.
